newsitem.title: FRANCE: France studies Credit Lyonnais recovery plan.
newsitem.headline: France studies Credit Lyonnais recovery plan.

text.p: The French finance ministry said on Tuesday it was studying a recovery plan submitted by Credit Lyonnais but had no comment on a report the ailing bank wanted another 12 billion francs ($2.3 billion) in state aid.
"We are studying the recovery plan and discussing with the bank various means" to help it out, a ministry official said.

The state-owned bank, still seeking to dig its way out from an expansion binge that drove it to the brink of bankruptcy, has already obtained two state rescue packages and has said it needs a third to get in shape for privatisation.

A source close to the dossier said the money that newspaper Liberation reported Credit Lyonnais was seeking -- and which it said the goverment was getting "psychologically ready" to approve -- reflected comments last year by the bank's chief.

Bank chairman Jean Peyrelevade said the bank would need 12 billion francs to boost its solvency ratios to acceptable levels to sell it successfully. But sources said the bank had mentioned no figure in the recovery plan.
The centre-right government, which wants a fast sale of the bank, has already agreed to a third bailout but must decide on the sum it will give the bank.

A bank spokesman declined comment on the bank's capital needs. But if the 12 billion franc sum is correct, it would bring the total of state injections to the bank to more than 20 billion francs, or around 1,500 francs per taxpaying household.

The European Commission, which must approve any fresh state aid, warned on Tuesday it might not be able to rule on the rescue before the bank's 1996 accounts close in March unless it gets a look at the recovery plan soon.
The plan had been expected to be unveiled when the bank announced its 1996 results.
A source close to the talks between the bank and the government said they were going well but it might be "two, three or four weeks" before the Commission sees the recovery plan.
A bank official said a special "information" meeting of the bank's board of directors would be held on Thursday to tell them about the recovery plan. No statement would be issued, he said.
Liberation said the new money would be doled out in stages to the bank, which posted 21 billion francs in losses between 1992 and 1994, to stagger the impact on the state budget.
The government pumped 4.9 billion francs into the bank in the first rescue in 1994. A second bailout in 1995 hived off the bank's doubtful assets into a separate "bad bank."
Last September, the government injected 3.9 billion francs into the bank to offset penalties imposed on the bank in the 1995 rescue.
The government has said the final bill will only be evident when losses on the sale of the bad assets are known. But analysts say the tally could hit at least 100 billion francs.

Liberation also said Brussels was unhappy about the bank's slow compliance with conditions it set in return for approving the 1995 state rescue. The bank was told to cut its European network by 35 percent but has only reduced it by 21 percent.
However, many of the assets were bought at peak prices and bank officials say the bank would face big capital losses if it sold them in current depressed conditions.
The ministry official reiterated the government's hopes of selling the bank fast but said there was no timetable. The bank has predicted it will not be ready for sale before 1998.

Peyrelevade, announcing a first half profit of 67 million francs last October, said the bank had "crossed the Alps." He said he would be satisfied to break even for the full year. ($1=5.280 French Franc)
